notes.127v.37: The stanza is obscure and runs on past this unit; it is given word for word, not construed. 'aura ... á eyri' may be 'ounces for an ounce' or 'ounces on the gravel-bank' (where duels were fought). 'mǽr' may be 'girl' or 'me'; 'bǽri' is unclear; 'taura' is taken as taufra, 'charms'.

nodes.text: by an appointed time, and I will refuse all compensation
for your sons. Thorveig says: Most likely you will bring it about
that I am driven out of the district and my sons go uncompensated. But for this
I will repay you: you shall never have joy of Steingerd. Kormak says: That
you will not decide, you wicked old woman.
After that
Kormak goes to see Steingerd just as before. And once, when they are talking
later Dalla told Kormak to go to Reykir. Skeggi will now
lend the sword. Kormak meets Skeggi and asks for Skofnung.
You will find it tricky to handle, says Skeggi.
A pouch goes with it, and you must leave it alone. The sun must not shine
on the upper hilt. Nor shall you carry it unless you are getting ready
for a fight. And when you come to the field, sit by yourself
alone and draw it there; hold the blade out and blow
on it. Then a little snake will crawl out from under the hilt;
tilt the sword and make it easy for it to crawl
[back] under the hilt. Kormak said: You sorcerers make a great deal of business.
Skeggi said: All the same, it will prove its full worth.
After this Kormak rides home and tells his mother how
things have gone, [and] reckons her wish can do much with
someone was groping under the coverlet at
his head. He asks who is there. The person turns away, out to the outer door,
and Kormak [follows] after and sees that it is Thordis. And she has then
come to the place where they were to fight, and has
a goose under [her arm]. Kormak asks what this is for. She puts the tame goose
down and says: Why could you not keep still? Then
Kormak lies down and keeps himself awake, wanting to know
what Thordis is up to. She goes there three times, and he finds out
each time what she is doing. The third
time, when Kormak comes out, she has killed two geese and
let the blood run together into a bowl. She had then
taken the third goose and means to kill it.
Then Kormak says: What is this work for, foster-mother? Thordis says: It
will prove true, Kormak, that you will be hard
to help. I had meant now to undo the evil fate
which Thorveig had laid on you and Steingerd. And
you two could have had joy of each other, if I had killed the third
goose without anyone knowing. Kormak says: I do not believe
in such things. And he spoke a verse: I gave ounces for an ounce; the girl cut off
from the bearer; a god of charms appeared to me on two walkways,
these. Blood will come of blood; never offer
